source.title: Unveiling Language-Specific Features in Large Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: Bo-Yi Deng; Yunyang Wan; Yi-Dan Zhang; Bao-Song Yang; Fu-Li Feng

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses limitations of neuron-based analyses but studies language-specific SAE features, not the share of neuron poles with one or more human-interpretable jobs or the tested explanations of those jobs. Its own SAE results therefore do not test the listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE-feature monolinguality measurements and ablations, not measurements of neuron-pole job shares or held-out testing of neuron explanations. The rows below record related results on SAE features only; they are linked to no claim version. Results on steering-vector performance and code-switching are not rows because they do not measure a claim version.
record.test_reason: The study analyses SAE features (Gemma Scope, Llama Scope residual-stream SAEs), not individual neurons. It reports no share of neurons or neuron poles with one main job, no held-out test of neuron explanations, no attribution graphs over neurons, and no InceptionV1 analysis. It only asserts, citing Elhage et al. 2022 and Paulo et al. 2024, that neuron-based methods suffer from superposition. That is a cited position, not its own result, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also claim that the language features act synergistically (joint ablation of a language's top features has a larger effect than the individual ablations) and that gating steering vectors with these features improves language control. They motivate SAEs by asserting, without testing it, that neuron-based methods are unreliable due to superposition.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses layer-specific sparse autoencoders to identify language-specific features, measures their monolinguality, and intervenes by directional ablation. It does not use the neuron-pole audit or held-out explanation-testing method in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that changes in target-language cross-entropy vary significantly by layer. Its monolinguality measurements are shown at selected layers.

fits_no_version.finding: Top-ranked SAE features in Gemma 2 2B and 9B and Llama-3.1-8B show much higher language-specific mean-activation differences (ν) than a random feature across Flores-10 languages. The top-1 feature often dominates.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Residual-stream SAE features in mid-sized LLMs include strongly language-specific features.

fits_no_version.finding: Directionally ablating the top-2 language-specific SAE features raises cross-entropy loss on target-language text much more than on other languages. The size of the effect varies by layer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Language-specific SAE features are causally and selectively used for their language.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper's own limitations note that the experiments cover 10 languages and not some low-resource languages, that the SAEs were not trained on curated multilingual data, and that the steering method falls short in some cases. For the reported plots and comparisons relevant here, no error bars, confidence intervals, or other uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-version results were left out. Results in Sections 4 and 6 on code-switching and steering-vector performance were not extracted as rows because they do not measure the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: the Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and its shares.
All of it: neuron-pole shares across models and scales, including mixture-of-experts models.
All of it: InceptionV1 polysemantic neurons and recursive generalization.
All of it: the architecture and tooling explanation, and the interpretable-share estimates.
All of it: neuron-based attribution graphs without replacement models.
All of it: whether activating-example explanations predict held-out firing.
All of it: simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Relation and tranche agree with the reader's guesses. The paper's claim that neurons suffer from superposition runs contrary in spirit to V1 and V4. It is only asserted from cited work (Elhage et al. 2022, Paulo et al. 2024), and no neuron results are reported, so it yields no verdict.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit, its one-job/two-job/ununderstood shares, and testing explanations on activations not used to write them.
Shares of interpretable neuron poles across models, dense and mixture-of-experts architectures, or model scales up to trillions of parameters.
The InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose detection, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
The proposed architecture/tool explanation for messy neurons and the InceptionV1-sized vision-model interpretability estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons and their ability to explain behaviour without replacement models or reconstruction error.
Whether explanations based on activating examples predict firing on new examples.
Automated scoring of neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.note: This measures SAE features, not neuron poles or the share of features with human-tested explanations.
